<reason>CON (A) ran the more inventive and rhetorically sharper case: concede the harm, then argue the motion as written is mere choreography that licenses "$20 plus 18%" and creates a safe harbor crowding out all-in pricing. Its textual pressure genuinely bit — PRO did have to gloss "before the final checkout screen" as "any screen where comparison is still possible," and PRO's "quote the delivery fee right after the address" concession sat awkwardly beside its own sunk-cost story. But CON's whole route to victory rests on one load-bearing empirical claim it never grounded: that a timing floor entrenches deception and blocks stronger reform "for a decade." PRO (B) answered that head-on and repeatedly — the status quo is the real safe harbor (ambush with total impunity), a floor is not a ceiling, and written early disclosure creates a scrapeable, screenshottable, enforceable record that makes all-in pricing easier, not harder. PRO also anchored its reading in the motion's own contrast clause ("rather than reveal them only at payment"), which partially blunts the charge of rewriting the text, and turned the "homework" objection cleanly ("earlier math with exit still open beats later math with wallet open"). Because CON explicitly agrees mandatory fees should be in the advertised price — a world that satisfies the motion — its no-vote depends entirely on the unsupported crowd-out story, and PRO exposed that trap every round. CON answered pressure honestly and with clear A1/A2 labels, and its closing crystallized the gap well, but "freer is not free" and "don't license the second number" are jabs at a degrees question rather than a refutation of the baseline comparison. PRO used noticeably less of its word cap and repeated "early truth or late trap," which costs it polish, but it left the decisive comparison — this rule versus no rule — standing. That gives PRO the cleaner reason to vote, narrowly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's demonstration that the rule is satisfied by a menu reading "$20, plus 18% service" was the most damaging single hit, forcing PRO to concede the motion is only "a beginning." But the decisive exchange was PRO's inversion of the safe-harbor claim: "No rule is the safe harbor — today a firm can ambush with total impunity," plus the paper-trail mechanism enabling later all-in pricing. That answer left CON's crowd-out premise asserted rather than established, and CON's reply ("one legislative moment," firms will cite compliance) never supplied support for it.</best_rebuttal>
